Summary and Source: Argentina signed a U.S.-Argentina Agreement on Reciprocal Trade and Investment (ARTI), with the labor commitment finalized around Feb 5, 2026: Argentina committed to "adopt and implement a prohibition on the importation of goods produced by forced or compulsory labor," placing it in USTR's lower 10% tariff tier. This was directly verified against the USTR fact sheet. No domestic Argentine bill or implementing regulation has been found tabled yet -- this is a treaty-level commitment only, structurally the same situation as Jordan's Article 2.9 commitment, and is reclassified from "No" to "Partial" for consistency with that precedent. No Argentina-specific hearing testimony found in the July 7-9 hearing record. Source: USTR fact sheet, Nov 2025/Feb 2026; White & Case / Gibson Dunn (law firm summaries of USTR determination). USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 10% for Argentina, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (U.S.-Argentina Agreement on Reciprocal Trade and Investment: Argentina commits to adopt and implement a forced-labor import prohibition; treaty-level commitment only, no domestic bill/regulation tabled yet -- reclassified from No to Partial for consistency with Jordan's equivalent RTA-commitment-only precedent)

Source: HCAMag / SBS News, June 3, 2026; Baker McKenzie, July 2026; Walk Free, July 2026. USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 12.5% for Australia, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (Modern Slavery Act 2018 is a reporting regime, not an import prohibition)

Summary and Source: Under a Feb 2026 US-Bangladesh Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, Bangladesh committed that it "shall adopt and implement a prohibition on the importation of goods mined, produced, or manufactured wholly or in part by convict labor or forced or compulsory labor," per the official USTR fact sheet, earning it the lower 10% tariff tier. Separately, Bangladesh's Parliament passed the Bangladesh Labour (Amendment) Act, 2026 on April 9, 2026, a domestic labor-rights reform (forced-labor prohibitions per ILO Convention 190, anti-blacklisting) -- but this is not itself a forced-labor goods import prohibition. No implementing import-ban law found yet, so this remains a treaty-level commitment only -- the same situation as Jordan's Article 2.9 commitment -- and is reclassified from "No" to "Partial" for consistency. Source: USTR Fact Sheet (US-Bangladesh ART), Feb 2026; Dhaka Tribune, June 3, 2026; ESG Institute Bangladesh, 2026. USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 10% for Bangladesh, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (US-Bangladesh Agreement on Reciprocal Trade: Bangladesh commits to prohibit forced-labor-produced imports; treaty-level commitment only, no domestic import-ban law enacted yet -- the April 2026 Labour Amendment Act addresses domestic labor rights, not imports; reclassified from No to Partial for consistency with Jordan's equivalent precedent)

Summary and Source: Brazil's government (via gov.br/Secom) called USTR's preliminary conclusion "regrettable," citing its ILO-recognized record combating forced labor. Brazil's forced-labor import-ban bill cleared the Chamber of Deputies' economic development committee (~week of July 13, 2026), with revised text expanding scope to a mandatory human-rights/labor due-diligence framework covering all products; it still must pass the constitution/justice/citizenship committee before a Senate vote — not yet enacted. On July 16, 2026, USTR (Amb. Jamieson Greer) imposed a separate, final 25% Section 301 tariff on most Brazilian goods over unrelated issues (digital trade, ethanol access, deforestation, IP, anti-corruption interference) — distinct from the forced-labor case; that 25% tariff took effect July 22, 2026 as scheduled. The forced-labor-specific decision (a potential additional ~12.5% duty that would stack on top of the 25%, for up to 37.5% total) remains separately pending as of July 22, 2026, still expected around the July 24 Section 122 surcharge expiration — not yet confirmed issued. Source: USTR press release, July 16, 2026; CNBC, July 16, 2026; TechTimes, July 20, 2026; WWD/Sourcing Journal, 2026. USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 12.5% for Brazil, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: No (bill advanced through committee mid-July 2026 but not yet enacted; still requires further committee and full Congress passage; separate forced-labor-specific tariff decision remains pending as of July 22, 2026, expected around the July 24 Section 122 deadline)

Summary and Source: Honduras testified at the July 7 USTR hearing (Melvin Redondo, Presidential Office of Foreign Trade), announcing an executive decree creating an express legal prohibition on importing forced-labor-made goods with three enforcement mechanisms (importer declarations, a Ministry of Labour risk list, and binding customs opinions), and requested a 10% "bridge rate" pending completion of its own Reciprocal Trade Agreement. Honduras's Council of Ministers, under President Nasry "Tito" Asfura, approved the executive decree the night of July 16, 2026; it was published the next day as Decreto Ejecutivo No. PCM-014-2026 in La Gaceta No. 37,196 (July 17, 2026), citing ILO Conventions 29/105 and CAFTA-DR obligations. The decree (Art. 4) prohibits importing goods produced wholly or partly with forced/compulsory labor, takes effect on publication, and directs Customs to build the prohibited-goods list into its risk-management system (Art. 7: intercepted goods face re-export or destruction at importer cost); the Labor Ministry's specific prohibited-merchandise list becomes enforceable 30 days after publication (~Aug 16, 2026), with implementing regulations due within the same 30 days. Source: Official USTR hearing transcript, Day 1, July 7, 2026; La Gaceta (official gazette) No. 37,196, July 17, 2026, via leyes.hn. USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 10% for Honduras, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Decreto Ejecutivo PCM-014-2026, published in La Gaceta No. 37,196, July 17, 2026; effective on publication, prohibited-goods list enforceable ~Aug 16, 2026)

Summary and Source: A worldtradelaw.net roundup of USTR hearing participants (July 2026) confirms Jordan requested to appear at and testified at the July 7-9, 2026 hearings, resolving earlier uncertainty about whether its appearance request was withdrawn. On July 21, 2026, the US and Jordan signed the U.S.-Jordan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade (Ambassador Greer and Jordan's Minister of Industry, Trade and Supply Yarub Qudah). Article 2.9(1) of the official agreement text commits Jordan to prohibit importation of goods produced by forced or compulsory labor within five years of the agreement's entry into force, and to recognize and presumptively enforce US Section 307 (Tariff Act of 1930) Withhold Release Order determinations -- this provision was directly verified against the White House-published agreement text. Law360 (paywalled) reported separately that the US committed to apply the lower 10% forced-labor tariff tier to Jordan (rather than the 12.5% tier assigned in USTR's June 2, 2026 determination) once Section 301 forced-labor duties take effect; the agreement's main text states only that US tariff treatment for Jordan is set out in a separate Annex I, whose specific rate figures could not be independently retrieved/verified in this search, so the 10% figure rests on Law360's reporting alone. Source: International Economic Law and Policy Blog, July 2026; USTR press release, July 21, 2026; White House fact sheet and full agreement text, July 21, 2026; Law360, July 21, 2026 (10% figure, not independently verified). USTR issued its FINAL Section 301 forced-labor determination on July 23, 2026 (Ambassador Greer, per direction of the President), confirming a final tariff of 10% for Jordan, timed to replace the expiring Section 122 10% global surcharge. Source: USTR press release and White House presidential action, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Partial (U.S.-Jordan Agreement on Reciprocal Trade, signed July 21, 2026, Art. 2.9(1), directly verified: Jordan commits to prohibit forced-labor imports within 5 years of entry into force; a 10% US tariff commitment to Jordan is reported by Law360 but not independently verified against the agreement's Annex I tariff schedule; no domestic import ban enacted yet)

Summary and Source: The specific domestic instrument has now been located and verified directly: Trinidad and Tobago's Finance Act, 2026 (Act No. 16 of 2026), assented to on 25 June 2026 and published in Legal Supplement Part A to the Trinidad and Tobago Gazette, Vol. 65, No. 111, 29 June 2026, section 24 amends the Customs Act (Chap. 78:01) section 45(1) by inserting a new paragraph: "(w) all goods produced from forced labour as designated by the Minister with responsibility for trade". Section 45(1) is the Customs Act's list of prohibited/restricted imports, so this is a genuine, enacted, gazetted forced-labor import prohibition (designation-dependent -- the specific list of goods is left to the Minister with responsibility for trade to designate, similar in structure to several other economies' framework-style bans). This confirms and supersedes the prior entry's reliance on USTR's Federal Register final-action notice (which had stated, without naming the instrument, that Trinidad and Tobago "adopt[ed] a forced labor import prohibition subsequent to the publication of the June 5, 2026 FRN" -- the Finance Act's 25 June 2026 assent date fits neatly within that window). USTR's final action (July 23, 2026) placed Trinidad and Tobago in the 10% tariff tier on this basis. Source: Trinidad and Tobago e-Gazette (printery.gov.tt), Finance Act 2026 (Act No. 16 of 2026), 29 June 2026; USTR Federal Register final-action notice, July 23, 2026.
Official Forced Labor Import Ban: Yes (Finance Act, 2026, Act No. 16 of 2026, assented 25 June 2026, gazetted 29 June 2026, section 24 amends Customs Act Chap. 78:01 s.45(1) by adding paragraph (w) prohibiting the importation of goods produced from forced labour, as designated by the Minister with responsibility for trade -- a framework-style ban pending ministerial designation of the specific goods list)
